title: Jordan van den Berg on his journey from South Africa to Chicago | Press Conference
text: Hey Jordan, congratulations. Welcome to Chicago. Um, it seems like you've got a pretty unique athletic background with family members who are big-time athletes. Uh, we were just talking to one of the area scouts and he was saying that your grandmother was a swimmer, your grandfather was a was a weight lifter, bodybuilder. Is that correct? >> Yes. So, I'm fortunate to come from a really athletic background. My grandfather was a five-time Mr. South Africa um bodybuilder, best bodybuilder in South Africa. Compete against Arnold in the Mr. universe competition and placed sixth that year. And then my grandmother, she was a national swimmer for South Africa and she held multiple South African swimming records and represented South Africa in the Empire Games as along with her um her brother as well. >> Okay, that's very cool. Um obviously lineage there. I mean are there other family members who are athletes like yourself who played college ball in any sport? >> Uh no no ma'am. Sorry. This is my f this I'm a first generation in America. John, >> hey Jordan, congratulations. Um, can you uh, like you said, first generation America. Can you tell us a story of how you got into American football once you got over here? >> Yes, sir. Definitely. I've always loved the physicality of sport. I used to love playing rugby, wrestling, and I've always loved the physicality of it. So, started playing football my 10th grade year. I was a wide receiver and then transitioned over to middle linebacker my junior and senior year. It sounds like you made some uh several position changes over the years. Is that right? >> Yeah. Yes, sir. Yes, sir. I did. >> What What was it like just trying to find find the right spot for you all all these years? >> No, definitely. You know, my body just kept evolving. Like I was small my first year. I was a wide receiver, then middle linebacker, then defensive end, then DT tackle. So, just my body kept evolving and it's been awesome to play everything. I feel like it adds a lot of value to me. You know, playing middle linebacker like helped me with my vision, I feel like, in my game. Larry, >> congratulations. Welcome to Chicago. Um, I understand that you didn't start playing football right away when you came over to the United States. You played baseball and basketball. What was your introduction to football? Did you know anything about it in South Africa? When did you start watching it? Like, how did you get introduced to the sport? >> Uh, yes, sir. So, I grew up watching um movies. I I remember watching the movie where it's the um I believe it was the Eagles that had um the try out for and one of the fans ended up making a team. I was like yeah I had that on DVD so I'd watch that like over and over when I was a kid and I really fell in love with the sport through that. >> Sean, >> so what's your uh you know understanding of like how you can fit into the Dline here in Chicago? >> No definitely you know you guys have a lot of talent. And I feel like I'm able to bring some of the pieces that you guys um have, you know, I feel like I'm able to dive deep into backfields and make plays and I feel like you guys are a very aggressive front. So that's something that really fits me. >> Bill, >> thank you. Uh congratulations, Jordan. >> Thank you, sir. >> Two-part question. Uh one, what um particular physical attributes do you think lend yourself to the position? And then the second part is can >> Sorry. Well, can you repeat the first part? It cut out. >> Oh, yeah. I'm just wondering about um your physical traits, how you see those um playing into your position. >> Yes, sir. Definitely. >> The second part is uh if you can talk about your story of how you came to America and your cultural adjustment on, you know, like how that happened. >> Yes, sir. Definitely. You know, I feel like um I got all the traits you need for a defensive tackle. I set the all-time Penn State squad record when I was at Penn State. I bro jumped 911 and I um jumped 36 and I benched 35. So I've always taken pride in the weight room from I feel like, you know, when I was at Penn State, I never um broke into the starting spot, but I knew that my opportunity would one day come through. So I made sure everything I could do in my preparation. So I take a lot of pride in my preparation, sir. And I would say um so I was born in Jansburg, South Africa, lived there all my life until I was 10. and my family decided to move over with me and my brothers just for the chance of a better economic chance, just for a better future. Sir >> Courtney >> Jordan, two-part here, two things that have nothing to do with each other. The first, what would you say your best athletic trait is? >> I'll definitely say my explosiveness. You know, I feel like that's something I pride myself in being able to be stronger point of attack. Like with my brawl jump and my vert, that's something I really take pride in. Every day I'm training, I'm trying to go as fast as I can. >> And I believe I read that you own a laundromat in Atlanta. Was that like the How did that come to be? Was that using you using NIL funds? Was that like how did you start a business while you were still in college? >> No, definitely. Fortunately, I had my family's help for that. And you know, my dad has always preached to me that um life-changing money is only life-changing money if you put it to use. So, the first thing we did, we wanted to look for something that was passive income so I could set up my future because, you know, I plan on playing football until I'm 45, but you know, um you never know like what can happen in football. So, I just wanted to prepare myself. >> just to follow up on that, why why a laundromat? You could jump into a million different businesses. Why why a laundromat? >> I wanted to do something that would help the community. We're in a very lowincome place and we do a lot of wash and fold services for homeless shelters and everything. I just take pride in being able to give back to my community and it's also something that's passive. So something that's hands off that I don't really have to worry about. >> Last two, Pat, >> you interested in expanding to Illinois? >> 100%. with uh how do you think growing up over overseas and moving to a new place and having to experience that and find your way could help you here moving to a new place, you know, having new co-workers in all of that? >> No, definitely 100%. You know, my whole life I've been I've lived in a few places. I lived in South Africa, then I went to Iowa Western, then Penn State, then back down to Georgia Tech. in every single place I went to. I've feel like I've learned valuable lessons and I'm just honored for the everywhere I've been and I just can't wait to be up there. >> Last one, Phil. >> Jordan, you you referenced earlier about your body evolving? Um, want to kind of know kind of a chicken, egg, and egg thing. Was it because you were changing positions or was it because, you know, you were just naturally gaining weight? And then the second part of that, because you've played so many different positions, uh, what NFL players did you admire or grow up watching? >> No, definitely 100%. I'd say I I just always was um evolving. Like I always took the weight room very serious. So I was always in the weight room and my body just kept getting bigger and bigger and I always took my nutrition serious. So I was eating as many calories as possible and I just ended up evolving and coming to the point where I am now. Id say the people that always like that I really inspire and watch is like Jaylen Carter, Fletcher Cox, and um Grady Jarrett. So those are definitely, you know, Coach Simpson was my defensive line coach at Georgia Tech and he would show a lot of tape um of um um of like when he was at the Falcons. So that's something that because he was the Falcons Dline coach that we used to watch his teach tape all the time and that's something that I aspire to be like one day. >> Uh how do you feel about Grady Jarrett being here? >> I'm excited. You know, I'm excited to learn. You know, my my coach was able to coach him when he was at um when he was the Falcons defensive line coach. So, I can't wait to absorb all the information from him, sir. >> Awesome. Thank you so much.

title: Keyshaun Elliott prides himself on attacking the ball | Press Conference
text: Hey Keshan, congratulations. >> Thank you. Thank you. I appreciate it. >> Yep. Yep. I read that you modeled your game after Fred Warner. Why is he maybe one of your favorite players and what have you tried to draw from his his play? >> Yeah. I think, you know, if you're any type of linebacker, I want to be, you know, somebody great like Fred Warner, you know, one of the best linebackers in the league. And, you know, everything that he does, you know, from off the field to on the field is just elite. And you look at, you know, a linebacker that's a game changer. you know, anytime he's going to get punched that ball out, he's going to get interceptions, you know, he's going to be disruptive in the run game. So, just, you know, his overall disruptiveness is something that, you know, I want to take away from him. How is how is he getting all these forced fumbles and, you know, getting in passing lanes. So, just watching his game and, you know, a lot of it's just a reflection of how much time he puts into the game, watching film and everything, you know, playing playing before the snap. So, um, you know, a great guy to watch film. when you have 14 tackles for loss and seven sacks, how does that come to be in one season for a linebacker? >> Just watch a lot of film, you know, understand what's going on before um you know, the ball snap like I was saying about Fred, but um you know, I just it's something that I wanted to do, you know, walking into this past season was I needed to play behind the line of scrimmage just a little bit more and you know, I was you know, blessed to be, you know, have a great D line that was able to hold some blocks for me to, you know, go down there and run through some lanes. So, um, just overall just, you know, the amount of work I put in just led to those 14, uh, tackles for loss. >> Courtney, >> Ean, what were your interactions like with the Bears either at the combine or after that? >> Yeah, actually, it was funny. I was just talking to my agent about it. We uh, we didn't really meet with the Bears too much. Um, I remember at the combine, it was great. Great. You know, you have seven minutes with them or 15 minutes total. Um, so it was quick. I mean, you tell them who you are, who you're about as a person, and then you talk a little bit of football. But, um, you know, it was one of the, you know, lesser teams that I talked to. So, it's, you know, a great opportunity for me and, you know, me and my family are just happy at the end of the day to, you know, be able to, you know, go right down the road to Chicago. >> Sure. And did you, I mean, you grew up in Missouri, is that right? >> Correct. Right outside of Kansas City. >> Who was your team growing up? Were you a Bears fan? Were you a Chiefs fan? >> Yeah, I mean, I watched I watched Denver growing up. A lot of my family members are Denver fans. So, you know, I was a Denver fan for, you know, quite some time, but I think once you start playing football, you just become a fan of, you know, players, and there's a lot of players around the league that, you know, I watch and a big fan of. >> Sean, >> hey, Keshan, congrats, man. Um, >> thank you. >> Can you sort of just take us through your special teams experience and and how you think you can contribute uh here in Chicago on special teams? >> Yeah, 100%. you know, that's the first thing that I'm going to be doing when I get into the building is, you know, meeting with the special teams coordinator and, you know, understanding the schematics of it. I look, you know, at myself and I look at a guy that was able to lead, you know, multiple defenses for, you know, multiple amount of years. So, going into the league, I know that's going to be a priority for myself is, you know, walking in and, you know, be able being able to, you know, handle special teams, not just, you know, for myself, but also the other guys around me. So, something I'm super excited about and, you know, I think, you know, my play as a linebacker is something that, you know, translates pretty well to special teams. Dan John, >> a little big picture question. When and and why did football become really really important to you? >> Um, I started playing football about nine years old and it was just something I fell in love with. You know, it takes you away from everything else that's going on in the world. Kind of gives you, you know, something to do that's bigger than yourself. You build, you know, tons of relationships. You're a part of, you know, a bunch of different groups of guys that, you know, you are going to know for the rest of your life. So everything that comes with football and the you know opportunities it it's provided me with is just unbelievable and you know something you know it's easy to wake up to. I love you know the game of football putting all the work in the extra work everything it takes is you know just something I truly love. >> What's the setup you got going on today with uh with just the draft celebration who all is with you and what's it been like? >> Uh yeah we're down in my grandparents basement in Richmond, Missouri where I grew up. Um, but the whole family is out here, some friends, you know, just just close circle here and um, you know, we're super excited to join a great program. >> Last two, Adam. >> Kean, how did playing quarterback maybe help you as a as a linebacker? >> You understand the game level? You know, I was, you know, high school quarterback. I thought I was going to go to college, play quarterback. That wasn't the case. But, um, you know, I understand what's going on in front of me a lot. I can, you know, acknowledge, you know, how offense is going to attack us, whether, you know, we're in a different coverage. You know, you, you understand what they're going to do, do do and, um, it just allows me to play fast and, you know, learn the game fast. You just the things the amount of things it took to, you know, be a successful quarterback just translates over to linebacker when it comes to work ethic and things like that. >> Okay, never mind. Last two. Courtney, then Dan, >> um, real quick, just going back to the question on special teams. I know you played so much on defense, um, especially the last two years. How much special teams experience do you have? Like were you doing it much at Arizona State? >> No, I didn't I didn't I didn't really play special teams at all, but it's something we always practice. I was always on the depth chart. Um it's not like I was, you know, taking breaks, stepping over to the other practice field. No, I'm I'm involved in special teams. So, we're doing all the drills, all those things. And I think, you know, I'm in a great position where I can, you know, go play linebacker, but also play special teams. everything that you do in terms of, you know, using your hands and having a base, using your footwork as a linebacker translates over to, you know, special teams, especially when it comes to tackling and fitting up on people. >> Dan, >> you the Bear Scout was telling us a little bit about the the commendation you got for your weight room work. What all goes into to winning the Iron Devil award, not once, but twice. Yeah, it was actually I think I won it, you know, I was there for four semesters. So, we it's a semester award, so I won it three out of the four, four out of four, one of two, but you know, just super blessed to have that strength staff, you know, just translate, you know, my game, my physique, you know, how I looked off the field and what I was doing from, you know, my eating habits and recovery habits. Just, you know, unbelievable support staff over there in the in the weight room. But, you know, like you said, it was just the amount of work I put in ultimately. you know, I was I was there morning and night, you know, outside outside of just our organized uh lifting sessions. So, just the amount of work that I put in and, you know, I'm a strong believer in work works and you're going to get whatever you put in, you know, you're going to get out of it. >> Adam, >> Keshan, other than quarterback and linebacker, did I read you were an all state punter as well? >> Yeah. Yeah, I I punted the ball. I I learned how to, you know, get the turnover and do the spiral and um you know, something that it's easy to work on. you can go out there pre-practice, mid-practice, you know, whenever. You can just go out there and kick the ball. So, it's something, you know, I actually enjoy doing. So, um it's, you know, definitely something exciting to talk about. >> Okay, last one. Pat, >> what's it like being one of 10 kids? >> Oh, it's great. You know, you got, you know, relationships all over the place. Um, you know, blessed to have all my siblings, a bunch of girls, and a couple brothers. But um it's you know great and something you know I'm just blessed to be doing this and you know just be a guy that they can look up to and you know rely on that's that's the biggest thing. >> Where are you on the list? Uh so there I have four older siblings and then five younger.

title: Sam Roush has football in his blood | Press Conference
text: So, where do you get the glasses with the tape in the middle? >> I'd say uh Stanford tradition. Uh I inherited inherited that tradition, but you know, we kept it going and um yeah, just something we thought was cool. >> Inherited from >> uh Ben Yuri, so he's on the Vikings now, but uh he was he was a junior when I came in as a freshman and then you know, some guys did back in back in 2013 and uh you know those Rose Bowl years. You >> got quite an uh athletic family tree. Uh you ever met uh Merlin Olsson? >> Yes sir. So he he passed away when I was about 6 years old but um yeah you know I I grew up around him and then you know my my grandpa is his brother. So we'd spend a lot of time together. Uh they grew up in Logan Utah and about 40 minutes away is this place called Bear Lake and so we we go to Bear Lake all the time and you know spend time with both of them and he was a great man and you know somebody I looked up to in my football journey. >> Did you know he was famous and everything? Uh >> not when I was six. No he he was humble. Oh, what about your choice of Stanford? I know your your dad went to Duke. Was that a issue in the house? >> No, it was it was my own decision and you know my my parents were going to let me do that and I I fell in love with the you know rich tight end history at Stanford and you know those are guys that I look up to and uh at the time I was living in San Jose so it was a local team as well but you know I I really fell in love with you know the tight end position early on and um you know wanted to be the next Zacher, the next Dalton Schulz, Kobe Parkinson. Do do you have a sense of how Ben Johnson uses the tight end group? Obviously Coulson last year, Cole and then Leaporta and Detroit. >> Yes, sir. I mean, yeah, Chicago, you know, we're top five and 12 and 13 personnel usage and obviously it's an extremely talented tight end room and, you know, that's something that's going to get talked about, but you know, I'm going to come in and I'm going to compete and, you know, iron sharpens iron going to make the room better and, you know, I'm really excited to learn from those guys. Was that something you were kind of aware of going when the Bears called your name or is that since then kind of diving in on what this team can do for you? >> I've I've known that and you know in this pre-off process watched a lot of you know a lot of Bears tape and um you know you got some good tight ends and you know Coulson Leland text me earlier today and just kind of welcoming. He's he's a great guy but you know damn good football player and that's somebody that you know I've watched a lot of tape on. >> What team did you uh what team did you follow growing up since you're moving around a lot? Uh I I followed the Rams growing up. So my my grandpa played for the Rams for seven years and his brother uh Merlin Olson Hall of Famer played for them for about 13 or 14 years. So that was that was my team growing up but I'm a Bear now. >> Did you follow any uh Frank Wek uh you know being in Nashville? >> Frank No sir. >> Okay. Okay. You mentioned your grand was there last night with you, right? >> Yes sir. >> What was it like to share that moment with him? >> It was awesome. um you know obviously you know he he got drafted about you know 40 50 years ago but you know he was real happy for me and um it's cool it runs in the family and you know he's he's someone that you know I've gotten a lot of advice from and you know he knows a thing or two about playing in the league and you know what it takes and you know I really respect him and you know kind of his journey and him helping me through my journey. >> Did he tell you how he found out he got drafted? I'm guessing it wasn't >> No, it was a little different. My my grandma actually thought he was getting drafted to Vietnam. So, it was it was it was a lot different back then. Um, a little bit little bit simpler for me, but yeah, it's a cool story. >> What kind of advice did he give you? >> Yeah, I mean, you know, he he stressed the importance of film. Um, he's he's big on, you know, step-ups. I don't want to I don't want this secret to get out there, but, you know, he's huge on step-ups and um just kind of developing your your lateral muscles and your legs. good for a change of direction and um you know being able to move laterally is huge um in football and you know especially the tight end position where you got to get good body position to win and um you know that's something that I've been doing since I was 15 years old and you know there's some other stuff that I won't I won't put out there but you know he he's been really important and and you know I think of him a lot in this moment >> go ahead that that Vietnam thing was that like a phone call that he >> so he he got a call I think he was at his mom's house and and my grandma, someone told her that he had gotten drafted, but she didn't know, she didn't know what that meant and so she thought he was going to war. Um, thankfully he wasn't. But >> you're come from a football family obviously, but what would you have done if you didn't play professionally, but >> to be honest, I haven't thought much of that. um you know really thankful for you know the gifts I've been given and the ability to play football and you this has been my dream since I was a little kid and just so thankful for the uh you >> know whether that Stanford degree had you pointed in some direction. >> Uh I I majored in computer science that that was never really the plan. Um uh but you know I I love my time at Stanford and um thankful I I was blessed with amazing coaches and really appreciative everything that you know Coach Turner and Coach Bah have done for me and um you know it's been huge in my development >> obviously. Okay, you were one of six players at the combine to do every single drill. Why was that important to you in Indianapolis? >> Yep. I love to compete. I was telling coaches all week I was going to do everything and then I didn't even know people were going to skip out on stuff until, you know, right up right up in towards the end after we did all our drill work and I was I was like I'm not going to skip out on the shuttle. So, you know, obviously um a lot of guys a lot of guys forego that, but I I just wanted to get a number on the board and you know, I knew if I didn't like anything I could redo it at pro day, but um yeah, I I wanted to compete and you know, I get to do it once in my lifetime, so I felt like I'd take advantage of it. Being an inline tight end that embraces the physicality and the run blocking, it's kind of become a bit of a specialist position in the league right now. Were you aware of that as you kind of went through the pre-draft process and did it maybe take your mind to certain teams where that may be a good fit for you? >> Yes, sir. Uh blocking is a huge part of my identity as a player. Um that's something that I take immense pride in. that's something that I've, you know, worked on every day in college and, um, that's obviously where a lot of my value is in the league and, uh, you know, obviously Chicago is a place that's going to value that. And, um, I'm going to do everything that I can to, you know, play my role on this team and, you know, all I want to do is help the team be successful and I'm going to do whatever it takes to make that happen. >> How much do you embrace and enjoy playing on special teams? >> I love playing special teams. So my my freshman year I played a little bit of tight end. Um but you know maybe 15 snaps a game in college and uh I played on every single special team. I think I had the second most special team snaps in the country that year and uh that's something that I really enjoyed and I wish I got to keep doing it as a senior obviously um you know you play a lot on offense. It's tough to play every single special team but um that's something that I'm I'm really excited for here. Do you in some instances probably enjoy or you miss like that rugby you get? >> Oh yeah, that's the only time I get to make tackles. That's the only good situation I get to make tackles. >> Did the Bears talk to you about Durham Spice role or did you watch any of him uh last season? >> Yeah. Um yeah, we've talked about it and uh you know I'm I'm I'm just excited to be here and uh yeah, going to come in and compete. >> Other than tackling people, why do you enjoy special teams so much? Uh it's it's a great way to, you know, give back to the team. Uh the way that it gets pitched a lot of the time is, you know, this is the sacrifice that you're making for the team. You got to go play special teams, but um you know, I think it's a great opportunity to go make plays and especially as a young player, you know, that's that's how you can kind of make a name for yourself and carve out a role on special teams. And especially in the league, that that's huge. You only get, you know, what 53 men on a roster, right? You're going to have to have, you know, really really good players playing special teams. And um you know that that's where I that's where I see myself is making plays on special teams. >> You played for a head coach last year, coached in the NFL. >> Yes, sir. >> In what ways do you think that might help your transition here? >> Yeah, it's huge. I mean, it's very similar offense. Um we were in a real pro style, you know, run first offense with coach Reich and um love that a lot of play action. Um I think it'll I think it'll translate really well. A lot of the concepts and and plays will be similar. >> Coach Johnson was an OC. He was the tight end's coach. Do you appreciate playing for a head coach that has a a background as the tight end's coach or maybe does it add more pressure because you know his eyes are constantly on that position? >> Absolutely. I mean it it you know means we're going to get utilized and you know he's always you know looking for ways to put us a point of attack and you know get us the ball and obviously you know he's a head coach and he's going to do what's best for the team but you know that is nice to you know have someone that's coached the position. >> Got to your science too. >> Really? I I did not know that. That was pretty cool. coaching software. >> That's That's cool.

title: Logan Jones excited to get to work | Press Conference
text: Has uh Hines 57 reached out yet? >> Uh they haven't reached out to me. Well, maybe they have. I don't know. I've been on my phone all day, but I had no idea that was a thing until after the the whole pick went down. So, that's pretty cool. >> Just about everything I eat. I feel like fries, burger. I don't know if I could say hot dog here, but um yeah, just about everything. So, >> what is Oh, go ahead. like coming here, going through everything and seeing this facility. >> It it's been awesome. You know, I was I was fortunate to be able to have a 30 visit here and just talk and meet with the coaches. Um it just reminded me a lot of Iowa, just the culture, the people. Like it truly is a special place. I can just tell. Um and I'm just so fortunate and you know, I was hoping I I'd get the call and, you know, be able to come play here. So to be able to do that, it's a dream come true. So, >> has there been any conversation with any of the coaches about playing here? What the plan is in terms of maybe get ready, take over the spot next year or go earn the starting spot this year. >> Yeah, I think the mindset, you know, you always prepare as if you're a starter, right? And obviously Garrett Bradberry's here. He's been in the league for a long time, you know, and you got a bunch of other guards, you know, doing Hall of Famer, right? Like I just get to learn from them and ask them questions. And obviously there's a competition part of it, right? you both compete. Iron sharpens iron type thing. Um, so, you know, we'll both get better for it and, you know, I'm just going to come in and work as hard as I can. >> Is there any particular uh center that you admired uh growing up? >> Uh, really the one that I watched, um, you know, being at Iowa's Tyler Linderbomb, you know, both played at Iowa, he was he switched over from Dline to O line just like I did and just seeing the way he he handled his business, the way he operated and the way he played the game. He's somebody I looked up to for sure. How does playing center at Iowa with sort of a pro style offense, how how did that prepare you for for the NFL? >> Yeah, you know, Coach Fence and Coach Barnett, um they're very they prioritize offensive line play. You know, Coach Ference, um he's coached offensive line for a long time and really thinks that's important. You look at the guys that have come through there. Um and I was fortunate to be able to play there, right? Um, you know, I just think the way they go about their business, uh, it's like an NFL, you know, organization and coach Fence coached in the NFL, too. So, I think that's where he got it from. But just very professional in your approach towards everything you do and the way you practice. Um, it was never as much about the on the- field stuff, but the off the- field stuff, how you handle your business and your approach. >> How much time did you spend like connecting with the quarterbacks that you work there, whether it's in team meetings, individually, just getting on the same page so things work smoothly on game day? Yeah. Uh, you know, I was fortunate the quarterbacks I played with, you know, I was all I was very close with all of them, you know, whether it be like a trip down to the the lake or something like that, but just communication, right? Like, uh, we we wanted to take as much off the quarterback's plate so he can just go out there and play, you know, he already has so much on to do and handle. So, if I can take a little bit off him and, you know, get the points and things like that, makes life easier. So, um, as long as we're on the same page and communicating, uh, we'll be all right. >> What do you expect to be the biggest adjustment? What do you expect to be the biggest adjustment moving from college to the NFL? >> Yeah, I mean the playbook, you know, after talking with coaches seems like there's a little bit more on the center plate here, which is exciting, and just the terminology, learning all that. Um, and just being in a new setting, right? Meeting new guys. Um, and you know, being a center, you got to be able to go up there, make a call, and be confident and have the guys around you trust you. And that's something you got to earn. So, it's like being a freshman again. You got to come in, earn the trust of everybody, and uh, it'll be fun. I look forward to it. your thoughts on re thoughts on reuniting with Tori Taylor. >> It'll be cool. I haven't talked to Tori in a while. Uh so it'll be cool to see him and talk to him. Yeah. >> You're you're going to be 25, right? >> Yep. >> Married. >> Got married. Yeah. >> What sort of stepping into a new job kind of from that premature point in your life? How do you think that helps you? You know, one of the Bear Scouts was saying the other day because of NIL, you know, the NFL is going to start getting, you know, older rookies kind of over the next couple years. Do you think that you're prepared now the way you wouldn't have been at 21, 22, stuff like that? >> Absolutely. And I like going back to Coach Ference and the way he runs his program like he just helped me develop as a man and, you know, understanding like the importance of, you know, showing up every day, your like your approach when you show up to practice, what your teammates see, and just the things off the field. Um, you know, being there for what, six years, it it definitely helped me grow and who I was when I got there and who I am now are just completely different and I think there's a lot of benefit to that. Um, so I was just very fortunate. Yeah. >> So much goes into the job of being a center in football. What do you do best? >> You know, I you know, being a center, I think the most important thing you you can do is, you know, be a leader and communicate, right? Um, I think getting everybody on the same page is is very important. Um, and then just having those guys trust you and you know, even if I make the wrong call, as long as we're doing it together, uh, that's the most important thing. So, just communication for sure. >> Your ability to to play fast and to play physical, but also to do it with the mental part down everything you have to do in the role of center. What's allowed you to combine both aspects of your game that way? >> Yeah, I think just getting comfortable with, you know, the playbook and, you know, having confidence in the guys around me. Um, understand they know our offense and what's going on and I can rely on them and trust them. Um, so even if you know I go out there, I don't need to make a call cuz they already know, you know, where we're working and things like that. So just having everybody on the same page mentally, even if you don't even have to say anything. Um, I think that's what helped you go out there and play fast. For sure. >> It was a runheavy program and, you know, NFL is a passing league. How do you think that affects your preparation and development uh, for this level? >> Yeah, you know, I think, you know, like you said, we we ran the ball a lot, but you know, we passed the ball as well, especially a little bit more this past year, too. So, uh, and we transition to a pro style offense, which is kind of similar to this offense, which will be awesome. Obviously, we might pass the ball a little bit more. Um, so it's it's a great opportunity for me to work on my pass protection and things like that, and it'll be a challenge for sure, but I look forward to it. >> There's been some talk about you being a little undersized for a position, but obviously that's not a new thing yet. You've played at a very high level throughout your career. How have you managed to do so, although maybe you are a little undersized? Yeah, you know, the game's played on the field, you know, and people try to get all these measurements and things that don't matter. Um, but once you step foot on the field, you know, all that goes away. Um, it's all about your attitude, effort, and the way you go about it. And, you know, being physical, especially on the offensive line, right? Like, yeah, I'm going against really good players, but if my leverage and everything is, you know, pad and horizontal, vertical leverage is inside, I I'll be okay. Um, and as long as my fundamentals are there, I I'll be all right. when Iowa asked you to switch from defensive line to to offense, what do you remember about that moment? Was it was it kind of humbling for you? >> I think it was one of those things I kind of knew at some point in my career I' I'd be making the transition and it was hard, you know, just growing with the defensive line. Um, but you know, Coach Fence came to me after Tyler Linum had left and you know, seeing the success he had, I was like, you know, I' I'd be dumb not to listen to you because obviously you know what you're doing. Um, and it worked out, right? And it it wasn't easy at all. You know, the first couple years very humbling and it still is very humbling. Uh it's a tough position, but just continuing to grow and trust in the process, our coaches and everything kind of worked out. >> Did you know so much was expected of the center position at that like when you switch? >> Did you know how much work centers actually put put into things? Like what was what kind of a shock was that? >> Yeah, I think you know being young, you know, my my first thought is I'm going to be like Tyler, right? um it should be easy. Uh no, it it was the exact opposite. Um you know, I was young, you know, I wanted to play at a super high level, but I think the biggest thing was just my mental capacity for handling things and being confident and making sure everybody's on the same page. I wasn't just there yet, you know, being a vocal leader. So, that's something I had to grow into for sure. And that's that's, you know, the area of my game that I think early on in my career I needed the most improvement. Um and I'm still continuing to improve in that. So yeah, that for

title: Ryan Poles wraps up Day 2 of 2026 NFL Draft | Press Conference
text: All right, we uh obviously had three picks today. Uh Logan Jones being the first one. Uh good opportunity to add another center. Obviously, that's a been a tough position for us um since I've been here really. Um, so we had opportunity to bring Logan in and um, high character guy, really smart, uh, fits our scheme in terms of being able to run mid zone, wide zone, u, strong, explosive, has great range, reach and cut off. Really liked his tape, so it was a good addition there. Sam Roush, another really good addition at the tight end spot. uh for a team that runs a lot of 12 and 13 personnel. I think we're top five in both of those personnel groups, that was important for us to add a Y to the group. Um so we'll have a really strong room there. I feel great about that. And Zavon, um another versatile player who brings a high level of speed, explosive speed. Um it jumps off the tape. Another one that as a group we watched it over and over and over again. It was uh we think he has some special stuff to u really make an impact with the new kickoff that we have going on in the NFL. Um putting us in really good position to uh and field position and then obviously punt returner as well. Um can take snaps at running back. Has really good vision and and explosion and feel and then obviously can take the top off as a receiver as well. So we can do a lot with him. Um, and obviously when you pair that up with with Ben and press, um, exciting things can happen. So, I'll open up from there. >> What's your vision at center in terms of wanting experience in front of Caleb, but then obviously using a premium pick on a guy in Logan that would seem to have a an opening to to compete for a prominent role pretty quickly. >> Yeah, it's um it's a vital part of our offense. Uh, and it is it's not easy to do. Um, so when you come from um, a school like Iowa, you're taught the right way. Um, so you understand the communication aspect of it. You're the glue. You're the the the circuit board of that offensive line and and you help the run game. Um, he's been doing that for a while now. U, we felt really comfortable with with his intelligence and experience to come in and and compete. Um, and you know, we feel really good about Garrett being the starting center. Obviously, we're going to always compete there. Um, but if something were to happen, we feel really good to we're not gonna have a huge letd down um for him going in the game and and operating at a high level. >> Ryan, it seemed like defensive line may have been a need coming into this draft. Was it a situation where you guys just didn't view it the same way as quite the as big a need or the board just didn't go that rout? >> Yeah, the board uh the class um a little bit this is you know a little life at the back of the round. um it's different u but it's it's really how the board you know shook out you know when we made that turn into two had a good sense through um our research that that was going to kind of be a hot spot at the very top of two wasn't really possible to get up that high without giving up a ton and um at the end of the day we just follow the board >> on a follow up to Herb's question so you don't get an offensive tackle anything on the defensive line. So, what what's your hope or what's your plan at those spots right now? >> Yeah. So, the at the defensive line position, you know, books coming along. We have Dio, Sweat, um Shamar, feel good about those guys. Obviously, we have one more day, so we continue to add, but like with that that group is and what they've been coming and we feel like there's some developmental upside. Like I said yesterday, I think year two in the system, um we'll be able to take the next step O line wise, we have, you know, open competition at tackle. Um guys that have played a lot of football and we feel confident that those guys will compete and the best guy will win at that left tackle position and then obviously we feel really good about what Azie did before he got injured and we like where he's at in his recovery. So again, we got another day to continue to add um multiple ways to add throughout training camp and the spring training camp and in the season. So um again, we follow the board. It's it's hard to if to go into a draft and and just start picking at your needs and hopping around the board and letting all the good guys, you know, go by just because of of that, it it doesn't that doesn't play out very well in the long haul. So, um, we stuck to the board. Um, every class is going to be different and like I said, when you're at the back of the round, it's it's a little bit different than being at the, you know, top five, top 10 picks, and I'll trade that any day. >> This is the second year that you used to premier pick on a tight end. Do you have to have a conversation with KT about, hey, this is I mean, is the plan the plan is for all three of them to start the season? >> Yep. Yeah, we do a good job between Ben and I. we communicate uh really well just to give those guys a heads up and and let them know what the role in the situation is. Um you know nothing changes for Cole. Um our feelings for Cole doesn't change um again we're top five and 12 and 13 personnel. Um if something were to happen um injury-wise to Cole or Coulson all a sudden you're changing a lot of stuff you know a lot of game plan stuff that is kind of your bread and butter. So, uh, we feel good about that room and and the guys that are in there >> right with that with the center. >> Mhm. >> It strikes me that this a good sort of tension to have between bringing in a young player and having a veteran have to compete for the job. Is that that's the plan obviously, right? >> Yeah. I mean, Cole's Cole's locked in. I mean, even contractwise, he's locked in. So, um, we're always going to compete. You know, it's not like you just show up and your spot's your spot. But we feel really good about Cole's position on this team, his role, his leadership. Like, it's not just whatever spot he is on tight end dep chart, but his leadership and what he means to this team is we view him highly. So, that doesn't change much at all. But, yeah, you always want to add competition that brings out the best of everybody. >> With Tennessee coming up for 60, were you getting multiple calls with that pick? Was there any 57? >> Oh, man. Yeah, this calls are all over the place this year. Um this is an interesting draft in general, but um yeah, just some different opportunities looking at your board where can you get more swings and um we felt like that worked out well, put us in position where we still got the guys that we liked and and then we add a little bit more for tomorrow. >> You have a pretty significant gap between the fourth round and the seventh. Do you feel like you are you going in at least hoping that you can recoup some of that or do you think you'll be able to walk away with what you want with the four picks between, you know, the four rounds? >> Yeah. So, I think we got a five now. Uh yeah, so we got four, five, and two sevens. Yeah. So, we feel pretty good about that. Um we'll see if there's any opportunities kind of move around, but um based on where the board is, we feel like we got a good shot at some good players. With Rous, >> how much does you mentioned 12 and 13 personnel having Ben and his vision, does that make you feel how how much did that like help make you feel comfortable? Because obviously if you have Coulson, you have Cole, like there's always so many snaps for those guys stay healthy. >> How does Ben allow you to feel comfortable using that high of a pick on a guy like that? >> Yeah, just the plan. Um the plan in terms of what's important to us and how we want to operate. Um, anytime you have clarity like that, it's it's again it makes the draft process and player acquisition uh a lot easier. You're not second guessing how guys are going to get used. You can see the plan, the vision, and the clearer that is, the clearer it is to to pick those guys up. So, >> good. >> Thomas, pick you and uh Francis St. Paul both very quickly brought up Ben as a factor in his >> development. How does your trust in Ben play into your drafting where if he says he can do something with a guy or he can get a guy to fit a certain role that he needs >> that that clarity doesn't seem like it maybe has been here in the years past. >> Well, when you have that level of creativity and you can put guys in position to um really highlight their specific trait to, you know, create an advantage. uh you welcome that all the time. So yeah, his ability to do that again, it reminds me of where I came from. Um he has a vision. I he's one you look next to he's like sketching out plays and things like that. So um yeah, when when you go through that and and he can see it and there's a vision for it, um you have confidence. Obviously, you know, the players got to do their part and there's development things like that. It's not overnight, but anytime there's clarity on how we're going to use players and and and not only just there, but also High Tower with, you know, the return game. Um, again, all of these things can create an advantage and put us in a good spot. >> How do you view the with Savian coming in? I mean, in big picture with the number three receiver, how do you feel like he fits in that mix with Khalif and with Jade? >> Yeah, so this is a this is a tough system. So, it's going to be a challenge for him to to break through u with Khif, but again, we're going to open that competition up um for all of these guys coming in. I think, you know, you feel really good about the return um ability that he has. And then, you know, he'll be in with the rest of the guys to learn the offense. And how does he do that? How fast does that come along? Um you all have talked to our receivers. It's a challenging system. Um, so maybe that role starts small and it grows over time, but you know, I don't want to put a cap on it. If he comes in and downloads fast and is up and running, then then we'll see what happens. >> When you look at that, when you were watching him on tape, are there specific moments that that you can reflect on and say, "Hey, that that >> fun fun tape." When you get that level of speed, there's a couple things. I talked about it with Dylan, too. There's acceleration like it's that 0 to 60 where you can just like feel it. Um when he throttles down I mean he can take off um and get up to high speeds quick. Uh his ability to decelerate is impressive as well. Um and then when you are 190 195 there's a level of breaking tackles um and kind of getting through some of that trash. I mean, just, you know, if you go through his tape and and you cut down into the running back stuff, um, for his entire college career, his ability to run in between the tackles is really good, too. So, there's a natural feel, vision, and just overall instincts u that makes him unique. And he's one of those I've watched the tape multiple times, and you you're talent guys that come in the room and watch this and coaches get excited, special teams coaches get excited, everybody's excited about it. So, uh, unique talent and excited to see him operate and and learn and develop while he's here. Did you know that he was consistent relative to Walter? >> No.

title: Zavion Thomas bringing versatility to Bears | Press Conference
text: Xavion, how are you? How you doing? I'm doing good. Good, good. Hey, did I read are you related to Walter Payton and if so, how? Someone somewhere down along them lines. It's still a long way. I know what I manifested. So when I did it, it didn't really surprise me. It was more like I told you so to everybody else. Yeah, Xavion, I was just going to ask you what your initial reaction was when when that that 40 was over. That's That's exactly what it was. Actually, while I was running it, I had took like a bad step in the way while I was running it. So immediately in my in my mind, cuz you know when you run a 4 2, everything kind of got to be perfect. So when I took the bad step in my mind, I'm like, dang, I just ran a 4 3. But after after the fact, I was coming back. title: Sam Roush looking to make an impact in every phase of the game | Press Conference

What did you hear about him? What did you know? >> Yeah, very familiar. Um, you know, played in the league for I believe it was 14 years. Um, and then my my grandpa's Phil Olson, they played on the Rams together for seven years. But, um, you know, Merlin Olsen, absolute legend, Fearsome Forsome, LA Rams, uh, Hall of Famer, and then, you know, my my grandpa got to be got to be a part of that as well, and he was here with me tonight. Um, um, I I knew my grandpa Merlin. He passed away when I was about six years old. Um, he had, uh, cancer from asbestous, but, um, you know, he he was a great man and, um, I look up to him and my grandpa a lot. um making this transition. >> Kevin, >> hey Sam, congratulations. U saw you you've uh in your travels you played a lot of rugby. Um curious how that's helped you uh on the football field. >> Yeah, I think I think just playing a you know physical sport when you're young helps build toughness. Obviously I have my neighbors that you know I wrestle with and um you know bang around with but uh you know playing playing kind of an organized physical sport when I was in you know elementary middle school kind of helps with you know form tackling general physicality um you know I think it definitely translated real well to football and you know kind of contact balance >> and how would you describe um your experience on special teams and is that an area that you kind of um take some pride in? >> Absolutely. Yes sir. I mean towards towards the end of my career at Stanford I didn't play a whole lot of special teams truthfully just I was on the field uh constantly on offense but you know my my freshman year I came in I played the second most special team snaps in the country and um special teams is you know something that I'm going to take a lot of pride in and you know that's that's that's a huge part of the game that you know doesn't get talked about a lot and I think that's you know just another way that I can bring value to this team. Last one, Larry. >> Kind of stole my thunder there, but I was going to ask you about blocking and uh obviously everybody always talks about how many receptions a tight end has, but how much pride do you take in blocking and knowing that you're really not going to get a lot of credit publicly for stuff like that? >> I I love blocking. Um, you know, the O linemen are some of my favorite people on the team, and I love, you know, getting in the trench with them and getting dirty and, you know, that's that's a huge part of my game that that I take so much pride in. And um you know I I never want to let that go. Um you know no matter how many catches you have you you always got to come back to your roots. I feel like, you know, blocking is, you know, the gritty, you know, roots part of football that, you know, I feel like, you know, that's how you play the game the right way is, you know, putting your head down when you know you're not going to get credit for it and, you know, taking one for the name.

title: Logan Jones: Chicago 'just felt like home' | Press Conference
text: Hello, Logan. Congratulations. >> Thank you so much. >> Um, can can you go back in time a little bit? You go to Iowa as a defensive tackle and then you switch to the offensive line center. So, you know, it's it's been a journey, but I think, you know, the past two years for sure is when I realized that, you know, if I really wanted this, I just got to go out there and take it. >> Kevin Fishbane. >> Hey, Logan.
