But no, I you know, I think, you know, I just like I said earlier, I think it's just what makes him unique is in today's day and age, you know, guys that that work that we it's the things we covet, you know, guys that are selfish, that are that are, you know, competitive, that are all about ball, good human beings, good people, um good teammates, you know, all the things that we're stress. He's about everything that we want to be about and what we want to build here. So, um, you know, we can't tell you how fired up we are about this one. >> How excited were you to find out that the athletic profile at the combine kind of matched like the good tape because he had really good numbers kind of across the board. >> Yeah, I think that's that's always part of it, you know, and and and those things, you know, you put you got to put stock in it. You know, this is a this league is about guys with traits and um, you know, so that's definitely one of the the measuring points. We don't put you we put value in it. It's not it doesn't kill you, you know, but it just tells you when you got to buy things, you know, and and you know, when it came to his his measurables and and testing numbers, you watch him at the count, you watch him move live and how he sinks and bends and um it it kind of matches up and marries up to the, you know, third down value that we thought he had. >> Can you tell us what you like about Caleb? >> Yeah, Caleb uh obviously brings uh some size to the room, right? um good athlete, can run the full route tree. Um he's uh he's got some dynamic traits. Uh saw him at the Senior Bowl obviously in the combine. Had good workouts there. Uh big catch radius. Uh can really get outside of his frame, competitive kid, great makeup. Um yeah, so really really enjoyed getting to know him through the process. Um yeah, and we've you know vetted him from from Florida. He started his career at Florida. um you know, high marks across the board all four years in college. So, >> what is it about Texas Tech Red Raiders that you guys really liked? >> Yeah, it seems seems to be working out for us, right? Um there's been a few good players here from Tech over over the years. So, you know, from Jack, Zack to uh Jake and obviously Jordan right now. Jordan's pretty excited. He's he's been in the building a few times already uh tonight in and out of the draft room. So, it's uh it's it's been good. So you I guess you gota keep going back to where you found him, right? So >> how does uh how does Caleb fit in? You know, there's a a I guess a physicality uh theme going on here and and uh aggression and things like that. How does Caleb fit in with with with that uh I guess that mold? >> Sure. Um you know, we're obviously just looking for the best players available. Um, and he obviously brings size and athletic ability and the he's got the uh the movement skills to uh to to do everything we want in terms of the of what we're asking the wide receiver position to do. So, um there's really nothing specific there as we just build out this this wide receiver room. Um you know, he kind of checks just a lot of boxes for us. >> Does he have special teams possibilities? >> Absolutely. Yeah. Yeah. With his size and speed and length, um there's that's always on the table. Was the size and length a priority for this wide receiver pick? >> Uh, not not necessarily. It just happened to fit kind of where we were in the draft. So,

title: Jacob Rodriguez meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: So, you hail from the same school as a couple other great Dolphins linebackers, one current in Jordan Brooks, another one a Hall of Famer, Zack Thomas. Uh, what does it mean to you to potentially be next? >> It means a lot to me. I think, um, you know, Jordan has has given me a lot of words of wisdom, you know, as I've gone through my years here and then, you know, I was able to create a good relationship with, you know, Zach Thomas and he's been a mentor to me and he's, you know, let me reach out to him for any questions I have. And um it's just it's been a it's a really cool experience to be in this position to have, you know, guys who were in your same spot and now you know they're they're leaning into this experience just like you are right now. >> Excellent. I appreciate that. Welcome. >> Thank you. >> Isaiah, >> what's going on? Jaya Smalls from the Miami Herald. How are you? Congratulations. >> I'm great. Thank you. Uh, so my one of my favorite games for me was I believe that two pick performance that you had in the Big 12 title game against BYU. Um, I know you're a former quarterback, so I'm curious how did you how did that experience kind of affect the way that you cover? >> Um, that that game it was I didn't have two picks that game, but um, I I uh I feel like I could cover well. I think it helps with uh you know playing linebacker or playing quarterback and um you know being able to see the field a different way but um yeah that that one that was my uh other that was my teammate. >> My apologies. >> No, it's all good. >> Joe, >> hey Jacob, it's Joe with Palm Beach. Nice to meet you. >> Nice to meet you. >> Obviously Zach Thomas is >> uh greatly admired in these parts. um what's one thing that he has, you know, said to you that you can share that's been helpful? >> He's just kind of, you know, reminded me of um kind of what he went through and this process that he kind of went through and, you know, how he had to, you know, believe in himself and um just kind of hold true to, you know, what he's had and and you know, kind of what he's earned and, you know, you got to especially being from West Texas, you know, you got to you work hard every day and that's kind of got to be your routine. And so, um, you know, just feeding into a lot of the day-to-day stuff and and, um, a lot of that we kind of elaborated on. >> How do you get so many turnovers? >> Uh, I think I have great teammates who are able to be there to pick the ball up if I'm able to punch it out or leave pressure on the quarterback when I'm able to, you know, pick the ball off through the air. >> Thank you, >> Jose. >> Congratulations, Jacob. Um, I wanted to ask you, how much do you embrace the opportunity to represent the Hispanic community in the NFL? >> I think it means a lot to me. It's, um, it's a tremendous experience. I think, uh, you know, with with my family and everything that, um, you know, we believe in and who we are, uh, it's a big deal and, uh, we take that seriously and I'm ready to be to be down there and get involved in the community and be a part. >> Marcel, >> hey, Jacob. Marcel Jacqu with ESPN. Welcome to Miami and congratulations first of all Arizona State fan so I'm happy not to have to watch you play against them anymore but uh I know you're a converted quarterback. Can you run us through the process of I guess how the decision was made that you would no longer be a quarterback and how you were steered to playing linebacker? >> Yeah. Well, ASU got the best of us this year, so I guess I'm happy. But, uh, yeah, and the the transition started, um, you know, after my freshman year, my head coach decided to step down and, uh, so I ended up in the transfer portal because he was no longer going to be there. You know, I wanted to play for him. And then, uh, Coach Magcguire just got the job at Texas Tech and he had offered me as a a scholarship player at Baylor when he was there as a linebacker, even though I didn't play in high school. And so when he got the job at Texas Tech, you know, I reached out and my head coach from high school reached out to him and I had some buddies who went there out of high school and played for him. And so, uh, it was kind of easy transition, but it was more so, you know, as soon as I got there, it was understood that I was going to move positions and, you know, he didn't have any scholarships left. So, I knew that coming in that I was going to have to, you know, be a linebacker and be a walk-on. Um, but then again, you know, it got so close to before school started where, you know, I got to go to school somewhere. I can't just, you know, not start the semester. So, uh, you know, I ended up, you know, believing in him and and, you know, trusting in his word that he gave me and, um, I think it's worked out pretty good so far. >> I would say so, too. If I could follow up real quick, how long did it take before you felt really comfortable in that role on the other side of the line of scrimmage? >> Yeah, it took about a year, I think. Um, you know, at first you're really just trying to understand how to play coverage and how to play defense in general. And a lot of it started with just middle closed run to the you know play your gap and then run to the ball. Play your gap and then run to the ball. There was never really any overlap or any playing within the scheme of the defense. And and so it took me about a year to finally understand scheme and you know with my back to coverage now how to play in and around with people and how to communicate well because as a quarterback you're just kind of barking out everything that everybody has to do. Well now you're you're barking it out but then you also have to listen to other people and you know communicate that way. So that's what I would say about a year and then uh you know I think it took off from there. Got it. Appreciate it, man. Congrats, sir. >> Hal. >> Hi, Jacob. Hell havoc with the Palm Beach Post. Welcome to South Florida. >> Thank you. Thank you. >> Um, when you hear something like Zack Thomas, Hall of Famer, saying that Jacob Rodriguez is the best defender we've had at Texas Tech. How do you process something like that? >> Uh, you don't. I think um that's something that really has just you know stood out and uh it's hard to believe and uh you know I I take his word very seriously and I appreciate who he is and everything he's done and uh the mentor and the man he's been you know to me and to my family and um yeah it's unbelievable. It's super generous and super kind from him and that just kind of shows you how great of a person he is and why he's so admired in Texas Tech as well as in Miami. >> If I could uh change gears real quick before I let you run to the next questioner. Um, I'd like to get uh your thoughts on how proud you must be of your wife and what you could tell us about where she might be in the world right now. >> Yeah. Yeah. My wife is uh, you know, a huge counterpart to me and then, you know, she she keeps me on the straight and narrow in everything I do. And so, she's actually fortunate enough to be here tonight. So, she's here with me and um, the whole family's out here. So, it's uh she means a lot to me in everything that she does in her professional life, but most of how much she's is able to support me and, you know, hold me help me through this entire process. >> Chris. >> Hey, Jacob. Chris Perkins, South Florida Sun Sentinel. Congratulations. >> Thank you, sir. >> Hey, uh you do so many things well. You're a three-own player. You make tackles, sacks, force fumbles, interceptions. How do you measure your value to a team? >> I think u you know my I think my value is a lot of it has to do with you know being the position that my coaches put me in and I think they they put a lot on my plate and a lot of it you know I was either asking for or you know I was I was ready to take on that challenge. And so I was just really appreciative of them to put me in all those spots to you know get everybody lined up and and make them do what they do. You know we had a lot of great teammates this year and so it was fun for me just to be able to set them up for success. And you know, if we get those guys going and playing hard, then you know, all I have to do is just do my job. And so, uh, it means a lot. I think I'm a very versatile player. I think I can play kind of all around the field and do whatever the the team needs of me and what's whatever is asked of me. And so, I think that's kind of where I can add value. >> And as a quick followup, what do you consider a successful game? Let's take wins and losses out of it because I know you you might say if we win, it's a successful game. Are are there stats? Are there other things, intangibles that that factor into what you would consider a successful game for you? >> Um, I mean, I think when you're playing a team game, you can't really take wins and losses out of it. I think, uh, you know, it's a whole collective. You could play a perfect game and still lose. And so, that's why I think, um, you know, success is measured by, you know, wins and losses. I think you can you can learn a lot from failing. You can learn a lot from losing, but the ultimate, you know, goal of the game is to to be there for for the one and0 at the end of the week. Right. Thanks. >> Omar. >> Um, Jacob, I'm curious. Do you speak Spanish? Number one. >> No, I don't. >> Okay. And you said, especially being from West Texas, what's West Texas like? >> Uh, West Texas is uh it's full of amazing people and it's tough and it's gritty. And I think um being from around there and and you know getting to know that whole entire community, I think uh everybody from around there is hardworking and they do whatever it takes to provide and then feed for their family. And um it's something that you know we kind of took over this year is a team out there in love is you know everybody kind of comes from all around West Texas. You know we're we're the only school the only you know pro team you know within five six hours. And so, um, you know, everybody comes out to support us. And so, if they're they're paying, they're using their hard-earned dollars to come see us play. That's kind of what we need to do to repay them is is just put as much in of the hard work and the dedication that they do to their families every single day. >> Um, and and if I may follow up with that question with the question about your your wife, I know she she pilots helicopters. Where is she like stationed in the world normally? I know she's there with you now, but um I guess you guys live apart. >> Yes, sir. Yeah, we've been doing long distance and uh she she's stationed in Fort Riley, Kansas right now. >> Okay. Thank you. >> Yes, sir. Thank you, >> David. >> Hey, Jacob. David Fus of the South Florida Sun Sentinel. Again, uh I know leadership is a big part of what you provide to a team. How do you manage that as you're about to embark on being a rookie on a professional team? Uh, and maybe when do you kind of figure you start to take on a leadership role in the NFL? >> Yeah, I think um it starts with just being consistent. I think coming in and being the same guy every day. And I'm a big believer in knowing your role and whatever that is, you know, trusting in that and and believing in that, but always trying to improve it. And so, you know, the best teammate I can be is what I can be. And uh no matter if you're a rookie or you're, you know, a 15-year vet, you know, you got to have a certain command and certain confidence value to, you know, move around the facility and move around on the playing field. But a lot of it comes down to just the relationships that you build with the people who you're around and and the the dedication to them and and to the people who they care about. >> All right. Thank you. >> Don. >> Uh Don Williams, Avalanche Journal. Hey uh Jacob, I was checking curious to see what your interactions with dolphins people had been um in the last several weeks, couple of months. Did you have any inclination that they were uh looking hard at you, looking seriously uh at taking you? >> Uh hey Don, good to hear. Good to hear you again. >> You too, man. >> Um >> thanks. Uh, no. I mean, I've had some excellent conversations with them and it's kind of been through the whole process of, you know, I was fortunate enough to go to the senior bowl and then fortunate enough to go to the combine and, you know, you get to talk to them, you know, here and there. Um, it's not necessarily always official and always, um, you know, very serious. A lot of it can be just, you know, small talk and so, but just every single conversation, every single interaction with them was fantastic. It it was truly unbelievable. Um, so to be, you know, picked by organization like like Miami, um, it's unbelievable to be able to join join that team and and everything that they got going on and especially to join Jordan down there, um, would be would be awesome. >> Allan, hey, Jacob, welcome to South Florida. Uh, since I like to ask the hard-hitting questions and since it was brought up by Dolphins assistant GM Kyle Smith, I have to ask you about the mustache. Uh, how long have you had it? Do you consider it your trademark and uh is it a big source of pride for you? >> Um, yeah, it's uh it started as a joke. My wife ended up loving it and so, you know, I got to keep it and um yeah, it kind of took took the community by storm this year. it was myself and then a couple of guys on the team um who who had it going and you know by the end of the season we had you know little girls who were you know three years old or you know women who were in the 70s and 80s wearing the dark mustaches for games and so um I I don't think I can uh you know abandon it. I think it's a a part of you know who I am and um kind of just represents that that toughness of being a a Texan and so I I appreciate it but um it's a it's a good talking point too. It's a It's a good icebreaker and so I think it helps keeping it around. >> So you will bring it to South Florida. >> Say it again. >> You will bring it to South Florida? >> I will. Yes, sir. >> And officially I think you answered, but you did not have a 30 visit with the Dolphins. Correct. >> No, sir. >> Okay. Thank you, Jacob. >> We have time for two more. We'll go to Andrea and then finish with Chris. >> Thank you. Veril Miami. Jacob, uh, I wanted to ask you about your parents. We saw their celebration and we've read your story and how you had to live in an apartment with four other people. What does it mean to them to make you uh give this step and and make it to the NFL? Thanks. >> Um uh thank you. It it means a lot. I think um you know everything they've done in my entire life. So, I'm the youngest of five and so, um, you know, being the the the youngest and them always wanted to take care of me and be in my life, they they've put me in situations, uh, athletically, um, you know, in school and in every which way to prepare me for the future and for for life ahead. And, uh, I can't thank them enough for everything they've done for me, all the sacrifices that they made, and, um, all all the their generosity and their love that they were showing me my entire life. And so I'm just appreciative of them of who they are and what kind of traits and character characteristics they instilled in me. >> Chris, >> hey Jacob. Chris Perkins again from the South Florida Suns Sentinel. Uh fellow Texan here and um used to work at the Dallas Morning News Fort Worth Star Telegram. Been to Witchah Falls, spent time in Leach. How much does that Texas pride uh fuel you? The small town being from Leach. Does it give you a chip on your shoulder? Tell me about how that influences you and and and your life. >> Yeah, it definitely does. I think anybody from Texas will will argue the same. And so, um yeah, it definitely helps. A lot of it has to do with kind of the work that's being done out here, especially in West Texas. It's uh it's tough work out there with the conditions the way that they are. And it's a it's a tough way of life. And so, um, you know, if I'm fortunate enough to play this game and, you know, I get to go to work and and my work is to play a game for a living and I I have nothing to complain about when I know who people out there who are really, you know, putting in long hours and long days just to, you know, put food on the table for their families. And so, that's something that stick with me. Um, it'll stick with me from now until the to the rest of my life. And so, um, I'm so appreciative of, you know, the Lord putting me in that, you know, position to have that opportunity to to really, uh, you know, learn about, um, everything that goes on, all the ins and outs of being from around there.

title: General Manager Jon-Eric Sullivan & Head Coach Jeff Hafley meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: How's everybody doing? >> Good. How are you? How are you? Did >> you have a good weekend? >> All right. >> What the weekend you guys had? >> Yeah. >> Fast and furious. >> What you got? >> Um, how did the draft experience work for you overall? Uh, just the first month with you guys together. I would say it was collaborative, cohesive. Um, felt like we executed and I, you know, I think again, like I told you last night, I think we helped the Miami Dolphins. It was, it was a great experience. It really was. Um, we're we're very excited. I think I speak for both both of us when we talk about, you know, the excitement of the the players that we drafted, uh, the culture that we're trying to build. And, uh, you know, number one, they can play. You know, don't don't ever mistake that. We're not going to bring guys in here that we don't think can play on the field, but then when you talk about the wiring of the individuals, we feel like we accomplished what we set out to accomplish. >> Yeah. I mean, I just start off I I think John, Eric, and um that entire staff did an incredible job. Um the work that they put in, the process for me to sit in there for the first time really in a full draft rather than just on one side of the football, it was really cool to see. Um, incredible process, the communication, the collaboration in there, just sticking to all the hard work that they had already done and and watching, you know, the guys kind of fall in place. Um, it was really cool for me to see. Again, I I think he did an unbelievable job in his first draft. Um, very very excited about the players that we picked and I can't wait to coach them. So, just uh cool experience and really excited about the players that we got. >> So, there's this trend. And I think you had four or five sets of college teammates now drafted here. Was that coincidence or is that ever factored into the equation when you're making these picks? >> Purely coincidence, you know, purely coincidence. It's cool. It's a cool story. Um, but no, that there was there there was no agenda or intent there. It just happened. >> Speaking of agendas, it was or no agendas rather. It's hard not to notice that there's one particular state you seem to draw players from. What can you tell us about that? >> Again, um you know, we let the board talk to us and it's the best player available approach and it just again it's coincidence that that we had a lot of guys from the state of Texas this year. Uh they play good football in Texas. So, you know, I think that's probably a good thing, but again, there was nothing that was intentional. It's just the way that it kind of fell. >> How much of a of a priority was physicality in selecting the players? >> Uh it's always a priority. You know, I think we've talked about from the jump just what we're trying to build here, uh, the culture, the competition, and then on top of that, uh, the play style. I'll let him speak to the play style, but I can tell you from the moment that we started working together back in Green Bay, he's he, you know, he says that word or that phrase quite a bit and, uh, and the players adhere to it. Play style and physicality is a big part of what we're trying to accomplish and build here. >> Yeah. I mean, I just, you know, if there's one thing I told him when he asked me my opinion on things, it's one thing I I was not going to back away from. I just I believe this is a physical game and you need tough guys to play this game and guys who want to be physical. And I think if you look at this list and you watch how hard these guys play, I think it's impressive. And what really that that says to me, it's and I've said this before, you can find out if a guy loves football based on how hard he plays. you can find out how much a guy loves his teammates based on how hard he plays. And when you look at this, I I think we got the right type of guys and I'm excited to work with them. >> So, you previously talked about the quarterback position um infusing competition into that room, potentially dropping QB every year. Um how close were you to go in QB? Why ultimately decided not to? And where are you on the competition in that room right now? >> Sure. Uh good question. Um I I did say that and it came up a couple times throughout the course of the weekend. Um it just we felt like the better option was the other pick. Um just a chance for for a guy to get on the field and help us this year uh with where we are as a roster. Um but the conversation happened multiple times. Um I you know I'm certainly not backing off what I said initially. We we will take a a quarterback every year, every other year when we have the opportunity. Um, but we just the way that it fell this year. And part of that is we we like our room. You know, we're we're happy with Malik, you know, Quinn is is doing a good job and will continue to do a good job and and we like our number three as well. So, we're we're in good shape there. Uh, and just the way the board fell, it just it didn't work out this year. But, uh, you know, we'll take one next year, if not the year after that. I've got a question about um BPA and conviction and um BPA and conviction I guess over need and I want to see if I have examples correct here. You guys uh took Proctor over Ruben Bane when you needed an edge rusher but BPA and conviction. You take Jacob Rodriguez uh over uh Derek Moore and Zion Young. BPA over conviction and competition. You've got three. You had two starting offensive tackles. You had two starting inside linebackers. Do I am I reading that right? Is that are those examples of BPA and and over and conviction over need? >> Yeah. I mean, and those other guys, again, I want to be I want to make sure I'm being very clear here. You know, those other other guys that you mentioned are very good football players and the Dolphins would have been lucky to have them, but yeah, it is a best player available approach and there's a lot of conversations that go into it. Um, I just you don't you never have any way of knowing what your needs are going to be. You know, I've said that to you before and and I believe that in my heart of hearts. I mean, you can you can have an embarrassment of riches in a room and then you got a hamstring and an ankle and now you're going to your emergency board. So, um, we we took the players that we felt like were the best for the Miami Dolphins. Uh, that's no shot at anybody that didn't end up here. I'm sure they'll go on to have wonderful careers and we wish them nothing but the best, but we're very happy with who we who we took and who we wound up with. >> Was there a point in the draft where you might have considered German McCoy or did you guys have a medically red flag? >> Uh, you know what? I he's a wonderful uh talent and and a really good kid and uh I'm going stay away from talking about the medical of of anybody or any players up here, but uh you know, I wish him the best. I hope he has a great career. >> Can you speak to your process now of adding uh undrafted guys? Um, I guess you can get a handful since you already had 13 draft picks. Uh, and how much of that has already happened? >> Yeah, there it's it's going on as we speak. You know, it's always a fast and furious process postdraft. Um, you know, we have we have our targeted guys and uh and we're in the process of trying to lock those guys up currently. >> About how many might you have room for? >> Uh, it's it's a fluid number. Um, probably I would say eight to 10, you know, just depending on how that goes. One of the more interesting picks I thought was Trayori. The Dolphins have had I hope I pronounced it right. >> Dolphins have had pathway players before, but not drafted pathway players. So, what attracted you to him and how quickly how where do you see him in his development right now? >> Yeah, he's a he's kind of a very raw athletic ball of clay, if you will. Um, he's he can move, you know, he's he's an interesting athlete. He's got twitch, he's got speed, he's got good hands. I think he's a he's a mismatch as a route runner and uh and he should only get better. You know, he hadn't been playing football real long. So, um you know, that that was what was intriguing to us, especially at that value. Uh we felt like a player who's who's ascending and whose best ball is in front of him and uh and can and can be a problem for defenses in time. You know, I have a lot of faith in the coaches who are going to coach him every day to continue to develop him as a pro. Um, but he, you know, he was he was a somebody that we had our eyes on for a while and he fell to us at the right value, so we took a shot. >> Jeff, are there one or two tangible qualities where the Dolphins got better through the draft, whether it's um, you know, competition or speed or size or anything along those lines? >> Well, yeah. I mean, I think we added competition throughout our whole roster and I think that's what you're looking for. I think that brings out the best. And I mean, you could look at all these players and there's different qualities that each of them have and there's different reasons we like some of these players over others. Um, but like we said, competition is going to be the key. Uh, these these 13 players bring that as well as the guys that we have right now on the roster. They'll be here not this week, but the week after, and we'll kind of get them acclimated and then mix a team together, and I'm excited to do that. Do you envision giving Proctor, no matter where he ends up, do you envision giving him looks at guard and tackle on the spring and summer? >> Yeah, for sure. I I think, you know, we we'll sit down and talk, you know, where the best available position for him will be. I think ultimately our job is to get the best five on the field and however that shakes out, um, it's our job to figure that out. um extremely talented player who can do both, which I think is a plus anytime you have versatility in a player. Um I think he can excel at both. We we'll figure out where the best spot is for him, you know, soon as we get on the field. >> Speaking of versatility, you picked a few guys day three and Trey Moore and Kyle Lewis that are kind of viewed as tweeners, right? I'm curious how their versatility um will play a role in your defense. >> That excites me. I think anytime you can draft a player who can do multiple things, it's our job as coaches to have a vision for him and figure out where to play him or play him in multiple spots. What's a down and distance? What's he going to do on early downs? Is he going to be a stack backer on early downs? Is he going to be a sub rusher uh in second, seven plus, third down? Is he a guy that can line up as a spinner and pick guards and rush? Um and then you look at the other guy. Can he can he play outside backer? Can he play inside backer? Can you insert him in different spots on the field? Um, you know, the great part about our conversations is if you find a really good football player, and I mean, smart guy, tough guy, a productive player that jumps out on tape, I think it's our job as coaches to have a vision for him. And then I think it's our job schematically to figure out how to make it work for him. And I think sometimes coaches look at we're playing 34, we're playing 4-3, and he doesn't fit the scheme. I mean, I just I don't agree with that. I mean, let's get the best football players we can and let's figure out what they can do. And now it's going to be fun trying to figure out these guys as we watch them do individual and then we watch them play football to figure out how to make it work. Um, and that excites me as a coach and I've said that before and I think we've got a lot of pieces now to do that. And I just I was sitting there today in the draft meeting. I even showed him I was like drawing up different things different guys can do like that. That's fun for me. And these are really good players that mixed in with the players that we have now. It's our job to go to work and go through the OTAAS and go through training camp and by preeason, you know, we'll see what we can do with them. >> On the same topic on the other side of the ball, you guys added a bunch of players on the O line, tight end that really can play downhill in a foam booth and they have other skills as well, but you also inherit a bunch of guys that have excelled at outside zone scheme. How important was it to you guys to diversify what you can do from a running game scheme standpoint? Well, I think the guys that we have can run outside zone, can run inside zone, and can run gap scheme. I just I think it's the same thing that I just said. Um, the more we can do, the more our players can do, and then let's figure out what they do best and let's go get good at it. >> Jeeoff, we heard Sullie's comments on Chris Johnson, but I want to go back to some things you said about how you scout quarterbacks um at the league meetings. You know, the the three levels of play. when you're watching Chris Shantton play, you know, how did he fare at all three levels? >> No, it's it's it's cool that you remember that. I think he can win at all three and he can take the ball away and he tackles and he's aggressive and I love his play style and he can play inside. I mean, this was one of my favorite guys in the draft that when we started talking about him and it came time to pick him. I mean, I I would not have been surprised if he was taken earlier than we took him. So, he can win at those levels. I'm excited to coach him. He was here yesterday. Um, he's got good size to him. He's got length to him. He's a great person. He loves football. I am very excited to get a chance to coach him. When it comes to edge rusher, did you hope to maybe get one in in-house in the first two days? And then how did you feel about coming away with the two you did get here on day three? >> I I just wanted the best player available and I think that's the cool part about this draft and the process and really learning from him and going through this the first time. Um, and it kept coming back to that as we talked. It's do you take this? No, just keep taking the best player you can. and we did that and we stuck to it and I think that will help our team as we go forward. Um and then the other guys that we took really excited about them. I mean guys that have versatility um you know at the end Max has got a toughness to him that we liked. He's a rugged player. He plays really hard. Um and then even like a guy like Trey Moore, right? All the things that Trey can do. The amount of sacks that he's had in his career, the ability to play linebacker, the ability to play off the edge. I mean that's really exciting for us. So, I look forward to seeing those guys and coaching them. >> I think when if I can chime in here, you know, the theme is good football players who can do different things. And as you build a roster, injuries, it's inevitable. Injuries are going to happen. So, it's no different than in life, right? The more you can do, the more value you bring. Um, and that was kind of, you know, that's been our theme all the way through. Let's let's just collect as many really good football players as we can who can do a lot of different things, throw them in the mix, and good things will happen. You know, that that are also I know you guys are tired of hearing me use the phrase wired right, but that are wired right. You know, that that love what they do and are passionate about what they do and have leadership skills and physical and mental toughness. And you're not going to go wrong that way. You know, you can win with with with uh with that with that mindset and win with that that process. I believe that my heart of hearts >> and I think you know and I agree with Sully I think what should excite people and what's exciting to us as coaches I mean as I look at these names these are good not only good football players but a they're smart football players they're tough football players it's going to be cool to see this group mixed together u because I think they all have a very similar mindset and I think they all have a little bit of edge to them and that that excites excites me to start coaching. >> Now that you guys have this full picture for the draft class and you try to define the scheme, right, is does it work as starting broad and getting more narrow or is it a matter of starting narrow and then building it out once you kind of get a feel for the guys? >> Well, I think we have right now and you know, Bobby on offense and obviously I have a I'll have a saying that as well and in our defense with Shawn. I mean, we have a um we have a system that we're going to run, but there's tweaks within a system and there's evolutions within a system and there's things that we'll think outside the box to add to the system. But in general, we we've got a really good solid core foundation of the systems that we're going to run that are in place and we've already started teaching to the guys that are here because let's not forget, we've got some we've got some good pieces here already that have been working really hard and doing a really really good job. Um, and we had two really good days of mini camp out there. So, this isn't reinventing an offense or a defense. This is now plugging in players to see who does what best and creating some really really good competition, which that is what excites me the most. Anytime you can add add that, you're going to bring out the best in these guys. >> For an entire secondary that needs to be rebuilt, I mean, you you guys basically partied ways with just about every starter. Why only one quarterback and why one safety? >> We like we like a lot of the guys that we have. Um we've got to spend time with them. We have some guys that were injured last year that are back and we've got to watch them on the field and then um same with some safeties. We brought in some guys. There's guys that were here and you know we did we added obviously we added a safety. We added Chris and then really even getting Kyle who's got the versatility. I know he's listed as a linebacker, but I think you're going to see him move around and do some things back there as well. >> Um, when you guys talk a lot about size, toughness, versatility, the only player that I guess doesn't necessarily Well, I don't want to speak on the toughness part of it because, you know, we'll learn that over time, but I guess size and versatility. Kevin Coleman is the only player that immediately comes to mind that doesn't necessarily fit those. I'm curious what you guys saw out of him. >> Sure. It was just it was an opportunity to add some explosiveness to the offense, some speed, guy that's uh again versatile, can return, you know, help you in the return game. Um, and has been a good player in in in in the most competitive league in college football in the SEC, or at least in my opinion. Um, so yeah, it was it was just again an opportunity to add some speed, some juice to that position group. Uh, and a guy that that we think can can do multiple things. a question. >> All right, guys. >> Thanks, guys. Enjoy your weekend. >> Take care.

title: General Manager Jon-Eric Sullivan meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: Proctor and why you felt really good about him to to move back and take him over. >> Sure. Yeah, good question. Um, he's unique. He's rare. Uh, he's a 350lb man with unique athletic traits that can play four spots across the line of line of scrimmage, the left tackle, right tackle, both guards. Um, the athletic traits for a man his size are through the roof. You know, I know there's been some questions about his weight. It's well documented. Obviously, we were very aware. We did our due diligence uh with our resources. We feel really good about where he is at uh with that. And um we brought him in on a 30 visit. Uh I could feel his conviction and his desire to be a good football player and do the things that he needs to do to be the best pro that he can be. Um all I can tell you is that there wasn't another one in the draft like him. period. >> Do you envision him starting off at tackle? >> You know what I mean? That's I think I think I I don't want to pigeon hole him. We'll give them to the coaches and kind of we we'll get the best five out there. I do think he has the unique ability to play all four spots at a really high level. Um it's hard to say. You know, we got some other guys. Obviously, Brew is very, you know, he's a center so that's but you know, Pat Paul and then you had Jonah and Jo, you know, who knows? Uh and then and then Austin. We're excited about him coming back healthy at right tackle. So, we'll just do what we need to do to get the best five out there. Uh the unique thing about him is he can line up in all those spots and you feel really good about it. >> There's always going to be second guessing and wondering I think for people on the direction you go when you look at the situation where you had 11, you had Caleb DS potentially there or a guy like Ruben Bane, a local guy. How is that process in real time as it's happening or was it a situation where you were set on Proctor regardless at that point? >> You know what, uh the other, you know, Downs and Bane are marvelous players. Um, and I understand the question and I I think those guys will go on to be very successful in this league. No doubt about it. Again, we thought uh we thought Proctor was was rare. His height, weight, speed, production, the things that he can do uh on the football field for a man his size, he's an outlier. There's there's there's not many like him. Um that's it has, you know, it's no shot at. Caleb D's a phenomenal phenomenal football player and he'll have a great career and we would have loved to have him here, but we had a lot of conviction on on Proctor being a very unique player in this draft and one that uh that that we can build around for years. Um, you know, we invested in Malik and it was important for us to protect him to make sure that he has time to do the things that he needs to do uh and keep him healthy, you know, so that was part of the conversation as well. Um, so yeah, we uh we're thrilled with the pick. We're happy to add him. We have a lot of faith in the person. Um and and we think he's going to be a really good player here. You know, no apologies. >> You mentioned in the 30 visit that he was impressed at how straight you guys were. You said you guys were straight shooters. What expectations did you guys line out uh to him when you spoke with him? >> Yeah, it was more just a real honest direct conversation with substance. You know, we we we asked him to walk >> us through his time at Bama, the lessons he learned, the back and forth from Iowa, the weight. Um, and he didn't hide from any of it, you know, and he talked about his growth and the things that he learned through that journey. Um, and then obviously we have our resources at Bama who have been with him recently, you know, over the last couple years and, uh, and we have really good relationships there and, you know, things like competitive, prideful, uh, never wants to be embarrassed, leads the conditioning runs. Um, you know what I can tell you about him is, you know, I don't need to name name the coach by name, but there was a coach there at one point who was militant about weights. Um, he didn't worry about Proctor's weight. That wasn't an issue for him because he could handle it. Um, the guy's got 270 pounds of lean body mass. You know, he's just a naturally large human being. Um, but he's not a fat guy, you know, and if if you put your eyes on him when he gets around here, you'll see that pretty quickly. So, I say all to say, look, none of us have a crystal ball. You don't know what the future's going to bring. Uh, but we feel really good about what we invested in tonight as a as a human being, as a professional, and as a football player. >> So, you said last week that you guys run through simulations of how the draft could go. How many scenarios did Kaden fall to you guys at 11? Um, most to be honest with you, most we were good with that. Uh, now there were some teams that were trying to move up. You know, I'll keep those teams to myself, but there were some teams trying to move up and we felt pretty good, uh, at least about one of them, uh, coming to get him. So, um, you know, we're excited about how this night ended. Um, you know, it was an organizational decision. Our coaches loved him, our scouts loved him. All the analytics told you this guy's a unique, rare guy. Um, so I, you know, again, I can't, uh, I understand the questions and, you know, that's just the way this business goes. Like, whoever you pick, you know, you guys are going to have questions about why you didn't do this and why you didn't do that, and that's okay. You got a job to do. Understand that. Not mad at you for it. Um, but just know we feel really good about who we invested in tonight. Flipping to the other side of the ball, um what stood out to you about Chris Johnson and how did you evaluate, you know, the Mountain West play versus some of the other guys that play SEC, Big 10, etc., etc. >> Yeah, you know, when you watch Chris, he's got great feet, great balance and body control. He's physical. He's a big corner. He can play nickel, play outside corner. He's got ball skills. I mean, when you start checking the boxes for a defensive back, there wasn't really left. there were there weren't really many left. Uh there were none really. He'll tackle, you know, he's again physical. Um he's just got and he's got upside. He's 21 years old. He's a good kid. He handles his business. He works. He wants to be a good player. Um he's about the right stuff. He's the kind of guy that we want to infuse into this uh into this locker room as is Proctor. You know, those guys are football's important to them and uh and they both have edge. You know, they have edge to them. Uh they both in a good way reek of confidence, not arrogance, but confidence. You know, they think they're players and all those things were important to us as we build this thing out. >> For a second, you you said that most scenarios he was going to fall to you. What did you guys value in him then that other team might not have? What you see that you said he's going to work here? >> You want me to go through it again? >> No, no, no. But you said most most scenarios had him fallen to you. Sure. >> And two two tackles were taken right before you. >> Yeah. >> Um why what did you guys value that? >> Why do you think you valued them and other teams didn't? >> I don't think that other teams didn't value him. Like I said, I know one team in particular was trying to come up to our spot to get them. Um and there there was another that was calling and I have a pretty good, you know, pretty good sense that they were too. You I can't speak for the other 31 teams. I wouldn't even pretend to do that uh to be able to do that. But, you know, again, the things that we valued were the size, the athleticism, the ability to play bully ball. You know, all the things I stated. You know, you can't play through him. He's hard to play around. He could play four spots. He's versatile. Um, we just felt like he was a a unique player. >> You stayed at 11. Would it still have been Proctor or was would Downs have been the guy? >> Proctor. >> Yeah. So, you said last week you'd rather have two good players than one special one in terms of whether you wanted to trade up or down. What was it about Chris Johnson specifically that you said we need to trade up? >> I think it was the versatility and I think it was the upside. You know, we feel like he's really gifted. Uh he's young. Like I said, he's 21. We feel like, you know, he can play really uh, you know, he'll play nickel or he'll play corner, but we also feel like, you know, depending on how this thing goes over, he he'd go back there and play safety as well because of the ball skills and the instincts. I don't think we'd end up doing that. He's going to play a corner, play nickel. Um, but we just we had a lot of conviction on him. We got a lot of picks. We felt like we had the flexibility to do that because of some of the draft capital that we had. And we stayed whole, you know, we didn't we didn't we swapped. We didn't lose. you know, we started the day with 11, we got 11 now. So, felt like it was the right thing to do. >> You've gone over some of the individual qualities of the players that you selected. Um, in the bigger picture, can you talk about the trenches with with Proctor and getting a cornerback, which you needed, and and you know, starting off the defense uh with with a corner. >> Sure. I'm sorry. Just say that again. Um, talk about building the trenches, which you said is a priority with Proctor and then with with Chris Johnson, you know, you get a cornerback to to kind of build the secondary. >> Sure. >> Yeah. I mean, it just you follow the board, you know? I mean, you always want to you if you can help it, I think you always, at least the way I was taught in this thing, you want to build it from the inside out, but you're not going to reach on guys. You got to follow the board. And we felt like, you know, the way the board was sitting at the time when Chris was there, um, he was he was we felt for us he was the best player available. And and again, it's, you know, you guys know how this thing goes. It's it's subjective. You know, you do all the work in the that you can. You got your analytics, you got your coaches, you got your personnel staff. Um, and you do you do that for a reason. Uh, and when you have conviction on a on a player, organizational conviction, uh, I think you have to listen to that. That's why that's why you go through the process and and he was one that we had that kind of conviction on and uh and so we do what we did. >> You said the word conviction a a lot as this is your first war room with this team as the GM. What was that process like as the voices in there and and and getting to that point where you were all in alignment to make these couple of picks? Like what was that process like? >> Sure. Just a you know a lot of work by a lot of people as you well know. Um, and then a lot of conversations, you know, we we have, you know, we have multiple meetings, um, you know, throughout the month of April, throughout the month of March. Uh, we have February draft meetings, but we keep it all separate because we're trying to identify the outliers. That's the way we do it. I don't want group think. I'm I'm trying to eliminate bias, which can happen when you have everybody in the room doing it at one time. Um, these two guys, to be perfectly honest with you, we didn't have we never had there were no outliers. We were convicted on these guys. You know, the analytics did it here, coaches did it here, we did it here, and then we brought it together and we looked at it. We were aligned from the jump on these guys. We saw it the same. And I told you before, like, you know, I don't need the validation of alignment all the time, but it helps, you know, it helps for for a healthy organization. You know, at the end of the day, the buck stops with me. I take responsibility for every player we pick, whether it turns out the way you want it to or whether it goes south. uh it stops with me. I'm not hiding from it. I really like what we did tonight and uh you know it's the bottom line. >> In the case of Chris Johnson, how important was his performance at the combine toward either getting your eyes focused on him or solidifying what you already knew? No, >> it's a great question and be honest with you is very important. Uh somebody mentioned the conference he plays in, you know, you know what I mean? I think at the end of the day, you're always looking for traits, right? I told you guys before, at least in my mind, this this this game at this level is played by men with traits, you know, and he you watched him play in in the fall and he had all the he had the feet, he had the balance, he's instinctive, he has all those things, ball skills, but then you're like, "All right, I want to see how he measures up with those corners in the SEC and he ran real fast and he jumped real high and all of a sudden you're going, "All right, you got a 6 foot plus 193 pound corner nickel that can play three, four spots that ran ran fast, jumped high, broad, you know, all of it. And it just helps you come to a conclusion that, yeah, this guy's exactly what I think he is. Not only is the film really good, not only is the upside really good, but all the traits in the world that uh that that you could want in a in a in a guy who has to cover players at this level, he's got them. He's got recovery speed. Uh he's got short area quickness. Um all those things, you know, it shows itself on tape, but then he validated it at the combine, which gives you peace of mind. trades with both picks. Uh what was all the wheelie and wheeling uh high level of activity like for you and what do you think of what you got out of those trades aside from the players? >> Yeah, I mean I think the fact that you know I've already shared with you how we felt about Proctor and he was kind of our guy. Um, so yeah, to come out it with with with two extra picks and not really, you know, just free money, you know. Um, so, you know, feel really good about it, you know, and then to go up and get a guy in Chris that we had a lot of conviction on and not lose a pick, you know, still stay whole. Feel good >> So, what was >> last week? You were up here and you mentioned that you had a dream. You woke up to a couple names off the board. Uh curious if either of these two players were one of those guys. >> You know what? I I'll keep the names to myself that they weren't and and I you know for full transparency I think I must have been back in Green Bay because I was actually pulling a tag off the board and we have digital here. Everything's digital. So uh but uh um no it wasn't one of the two. But uh I think it just tells you about the excitement you know that that I had that we had. Uh, we've been talking about this day, spent a lot of time in the draft room, hours upon hours trying to get to this point and prepare. And, uh, you know, we're excited. We feel like it was a really good first day. But, uh, it's, uh, it was, it was a funny dream. I was pulling the tag and I I literally woke up and I thought to myself like, damn, I was in Green Bay. It wasn't digital. >> Almost kind of building off of that question, what was this day like for you leading up to the start of the first round? You know, first do you have a post note in your pocket said Kaden Proctor no matter what or >> No, you know, you you have all that time on the front end of the day. You know, it's like the day itself takes a month, you know, to finally get to 8:00. But, uh, for me, I just I think sometimes you just go back to the simplicity of everything. You know, you read through your notes, you look at the great you look, how do I feel about him? How do our coaches feel about him? How do our scouts that do a great job feel about them? and you know, you start weighing things out and and it it speaks to you. It talks to you. And look, man, there's there's a lot of other really good players that were on the board um that are still on the board. Uh but that's this business. You got to make decisions. Um and uh feel good about the ones we made today. >> For the record, just asking like your nerves, the calmness of it, like what went through your brain as you're preparing for this? Yeah, it was I mean I I came in, we met with our guys, uh I got a workout in which helped me kind of clear my head and then uh I mean and this is this is just the truth of it. There there was an eerie calm for me like it's the work is done like this is the fun part. Now that doesn't mean you know things can heat up and go you know in moments when trades are happening things get going fast but you stay calm and you communicate and you and you you know you do what you need to do for your team. It's the execution piece of it. The work is in and has been done and it's like there there was a calm that came with the preparation. Uh which was I didn't expect it. It was pretty cool to be honest with you. I kind of I told somebody beforehand like I you know there's a like I feel like I should be more anxious. I'm not. I trust the people in the room. I trust our work. I trust the process. And uh like I said, I think the Dolphins got better today. I'm reading a quote here from the athletics uh scouting guide from a NFL scout who said that Chris Johnson's give a damn factor to the moon. Leader of the DB room, likable kid. His parents did an amazing job. I was just curious to get your perspective on your guys' background with Chris Johnson. >> Yeah, everything you just said, you know, we did a lot of work on him like we do on all the players. Um the coaches San Diego State couldn't have said better things about him. His care factor is high. He was a captain, team captain there. He's a leader. Uh he works. Um the intangibles along with the athletic traits along with the fact that he's a good football player lead to the conviction why we did what we did. You know that's uh you know I I told you guys from the jump you know um it's important that we we had the right kind of people here and Proctor's in that I mean you know he didn't hide from it and he's we feel like he's going this way and so do the people who've been around him you know over the last couple years. Um, these these are young people. Young people make mistakes. They have bumps in the roads. If I peel the layers back on all you guys when you were young, I know I made my mistakes. I'm sure y'all did, too. These kids aren't any different, you know? They're no different, you know, and they and they deserve, you can't bury them because they stubbed their toe along the way. I mean, there's certain things you won't forgive, but a guy who's, you know, battled his weight a little bit here and there and has gotten together and played really good football, you know, you got to give guys their due and see where they're going, not where they've been all the time in my opinion. >> I heard a coach say the other day that your first round pick or first round picks in your case are supposed to change the tone of practice. How do you I don't know if you I don't know if you subscribe to that, but how do you believe these two guys kind of change the the tone of practice? >> Sure. Um you know, I I think with Proctor when he walks out there, he's going to change the tone of practice. uh just with his size and his mass and I I think when when when you see people try to when they run into him and he you know the stopping power that he has, the ability to move uh large men coming off the ball in the run game um you know that'll speak for itself, you know. Um, and again, I I just I think the I think the raw athleticism of of of Johnson and again his ability to be versatile uh with his athletic traits and his mental, you know, smarts, you know, I think I think they'll recogn I think the team will recognize that pretty quick and respect it. You know, that's what I would say. >> So, as you look >> as you look to day two, is it still best player available or do you feel some needs? >> No, it's uh need comes into play. Hey, I mean, we'll always follow the board in terms of value, but you know, if you're looking at two guys that have the same value and and and you need one more, then it comes into play. That makes sense, you know. Um, got to, you know, yes, there there there do there does come a point where you're trying to fill holes, but you're not going to not follow the value of the board. >> There's obviously high expectations, you know, obviously based on what you said about Parker. How much do you have to help him understand and not this conversation from the outside get to his head and put even more pressure on him to perform? >> Yeah, you know, I mean, it's a good question. I think part part of it when you when you when you draft these guys, you have faith in our I have faith in our building and the people in this building. I have faith in Coach Hafley. I have faith in Coach Yenszer. have faith in, you know, our nutritionists and our strength staff and all the people that come to work here every day that are really good at their job. Um, you know, every I said this to our the first and I hate to use the word speech, but the first talk I gave to the building, like we all have a job to do and nobody here is more important than the other. Like we all have a role in this thing to get this place where we need it to get to. Um, and that's part of it. Like that's why you have a building full of people that have different jobs is to help these players be the best that they can be. And I have a lot of faith in this building and the people that come to work here every day. I also have faith in him that he's going to do the things that he needs to do. So um you know and he's been at Bama, you know what I mean? He's been at Bama and he's been out there every week playing uh you know he lined up every you know every Saturday and played good ball. You know go watch the tape. I mean it's that's you know I'll sit down and watch the tape with any of you if you want to. You tell me. >> Is that an opening business? >> Yeah, I was about to say >> at some point tomorrow. >> All right, y'all have a good night. See you. Take it easy.

title: Jaren Kanak Talks About Joining the Tennessee Titans | Press Conference
text: Jaren, congratulations on being chosen by the Titans. What went into the whole process of switching from linebacker to tight end last year for the Sooners? Yeah, definitely. So, I I grew up my entire life I was an offensive player and it was it was kind of just coming out I was I was recruited at the college level as more of a defensive, you know, style player and that's what I did my first 3 years, but you know, I kind of got to a position in my career in my junior year of college where I kind of realized that that maybe defense wasn't for me and I I basically just approached coaches in the off-season and said, "Hey, listen, I got the offensive background. I'm kind of hitting a wall in my career here on defense and you know, I really think I might be able to offer more to this team if if you let me try out offense." You know, I was just I was just trying to find a place where I could add value to the team and you know, be a guy that was able to lead us towards success. So, they gave me the opportunity to switch over in the spring. They gave me a spring to try it out and you know, it ended up working out pretty well for me. As far as your mentality on the defensive side of the ball, taking that to offense, what all did you kind of take over there to that side of the ball when you were moved there? Yeah, I mean, obviously playing linebacker you kind of have a a little bit of an edge to you. There's a little more tenacity there. Obviously, you play the the game in an aggressive style manner and that that's something I like to do. Jaren, you said you hit a wall as a defensive player and that you, you know, mentioning your offensive background, you played quarterback in high school. How did that help you make that transition to tight end and how do you feel like that's, you know, going to help you as you transition to the NFL level? Yeah, definitely. You said obviously playing quarterback you have a very, you know, holistic understanding of of what goes on in an offense, an offensive scheme and then having that defensive background as well in the in the system that I was in with Coach Brent Venables. It was a very holistic system as well where you you needed understanding of everything that was going on around you and to to make everything work. And so, having having that that that mindset and understanding of the whole concept of of any given play is is really going to help me moving forward. And it has really helped me.
